title: Regret–Oracle Complexity Tradeoffs in Agnostic Online Learning
claim: We sharply cut the query cost of near-optimal regret and map the achievable, impossible, and still-open regimes.
layout: 1 annotated plot, axes regret vs queries, shaded regions with colored labels
description: A schematic plot of expected regret on the y-axis against total oracle queries Q on the x-axis, with labeled tick values such as O(T), O(√T), O(T^{d_VC+1}) and O(T^{2^{O(d_LD)}}). Three shaded regions fill the plot. A light green region at upper right is the achievable region (upper bounds). A pale yellow region at upper left is the open gap, marked by a downward arrow. A gray region at the bottom is the impossible region (lower bounds). Green lines and dots mark the new results: a dashed query-budget lower bound Ω(T/Q) and a solid tradeoff frontier. Algorithm 2 sits as a green dot on the horizontal dashed orange line, which is the prior bound. A blue curved arrow runs from the orange prior upper-bound dot to the green dot. It is labeled as an exponential or double-exponential query reduction that keeps the same regret. Theorem labels appear in white boxes.
caption: Expected regret vs. total oracle queries tradeoff. Our results are marked in green, whereas previous results appear in orange. The yellow region highlights the gap between the known upper and lower bounds. We believe that closing this gap will require fundamentally new ideas, potentially including oracle-efficient algorithms for agnostic online learning that go beyond the agnostic-to-realizable reduction, stronger query-budget lower bounds, or both.
abstract: Agnostic online learning is classically solved via a reduction to the realizable setting, utilizing Littlestone's Standard Optimal Algorithm (SOA) as a base learner. However, the SOA can be computationally intractable to implement even for a single round. To overcome this barrier, recent work in oracle-efficient online learning replaces the SOA with a realizable base learner that accesses the concept class exclusively through an offline empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. While such agnostic learners achieve expected regret $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(\sqrt{T\cdot 2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$, which is near-optimal in the horizon $T$ for fixed Littlestone dimension $d_{\mathrm{LD}}$, they require $\mathcal{O}\big(T^{2^{\mathcal{O}(d_{\mathrm{LD}})}}\big)$ oracle calls. In this work, we significantly improve this oracle complexity while relying on an even weaker primitive: a weak-consistency oracle, which merely decides whether a given labeled dataset is realizable. At the core of our approach is an adaptive and dynamic agnostic-to-realizable reduction that actively prunes non-realizable label sequences on the fly. By using the VC dimension ($d_{\mathrm{VC}}$) to bound the number of dynamically maintained active paths, our algorithm reduces the total query complexity down to $\mathcal{O}(T^{d_{\mathrm{VC}}+1})$ while perfectly preserving near-optimal expected regret. Crucially, this dynamic pruning also yields a memory reduction over the standard reduction. Furthermore, we formally quantify the regret--oracle complexity tradeoff, providing upper bounds that smoothly interpolate between restricted query budgets and attainable expected regret. We complement these with lower bounds proving that any learner restricted to $Q = o(\sqrt{T})$ queries must suffer an expected regret of $Î©(T/Q)$.
